subject: Principles of Flight
question_text: What is the angle of attack of a wing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The angle between the chord line and the relative airflow

choices.label: B
choices.text: The angle between the chord line and the aeroplane's longitudinal axis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon

choices.label: D
choices.text: The angle between the flight path and the horizon

explanation: Angle of attack is measured between the chord line and the relative airflow (free-stream direction). It, not attitude, determines the lift coefficient and the stall.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: That is the angle of incidence, a fixed rigging angle.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That is the pitch attitude, which can differ from the angle of attack.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That is the flight-path (climb or descent) angle.

subject: Principles of Flight
learning_objective: Relate the stall to the critical angle of attack
question_text: Under which condition does a wing stall?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only when the airspeed falls below the published stall speed

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the critical angle of attack is exceeded, at any airspeed or attitude

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only when the nose is pitched above the horizon

choices.label: D
choices.text: When the engine power is reduced to idle

explanation: The airflow separates from the upper surface once the critical angle of attack (typically around 15-18 degrees for a light-aircraft aerofoil) is exceeded, whatever the airspeed, attitude or power.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Published stall speeds apply only to 1 g wings-level flight at a given mass and configuration; a wing can stall above them, e.g. in a steep turn or abrupt pull-up.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Attitude does not cause the stall; a wing can stall in a nose-down attitude if the angle of attack is excessive.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Power reduction alone does not stall a wing; the angle of attack does.

subject: Principles of Flight
learning_objective: Calculate the stall speed in a level turn
question_text: An aeroplane has a wings-level stall speed of 50 kt. What is its approximate stall speed in a level, coordinated turn at 60 degrees of bank?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 50 kt

choices.label: B
choices.text: 100 kt

choices.label: C
choices.text: 71 kt

choices.label: D
choices.text: 58 kt

explanation: In a level turn the load factor n = 1/cos(bank). At 60 degrees n = 2, and stall speed rises by the square root of n: 50 x 1.414 = 70.7, about 71 kt.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Stall speed increases in a level turn because the load factor rises.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor (2), not with the load factor itself.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That would correspond to a load factor of about 1.35, i.e. a bank of roughly 42 degrees.

calculation_steps: n = 1/cos(60 deg) = 2.0; Vs(turn) = Vs x sqrt(n) = 50 x 1.414 = 70.7 kt, approximately 71 kt

question_text: Compared with the clean configuration, what is the main effect of lowering trailing-edge flaps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The maximum lift coefficient increases, so the stall speed decreases

choices.label: B
choices.text: The maximum lift coefficient decreases, so the stall speed increases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drag decreases, so the aeroplane accelerates

choices.label: D
choices.text: The critical angle of attack increases, so the nose must be raised further to stall

explanation: Trailing-edge flaps increase camber and so the maximum lift coefficient. The aeroplane can fly slower before stalling, at the cost of more drag.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This reverses the effect; flaps raise the maximum lift coefficient.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Flaps add drag, especially at large settings.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Trailing-edge flaps generally reduce the critical angle of attack slightly.

subject: Principles of Flight
question_text: During take-off, how does ground effect influence the aeroplane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Induced drag is increased, so the take-off run is longer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Induced drag is reduced, so the aeroplane may become airborne before it can climb out of ground effect safely

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parasite drag disappears close to the ground

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lift is reduced, so a higher lift-off speed is always required

explanation: Near the ground the downwash and wing-tip vortices are restricted, reducing induced drag. An aeroplane may lift off at a speed too low to keep climbing once it leaves ground effect, roughly one wingspan up.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Ground effect reduces, not increases, induced drag.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Ground effect acts on the wing-tip vortices and downwash, i.e. on induced drag.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Ground effect lets the wing produce a given lift at a lower angle of attack.

subject: Principles of Flight
question_text: In level flight, how does induced drag change as airspeed is reduced towards the stall?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It decreases

choices.label: B
choices.text: It remains constant

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases

choices.label: D
choices.text: It becomes zero at the stall

explanation: To keep lift equal to weight at lower speed the angle of attack must increase. That strengthens the wing-tip vortices, so induced drag rises roughly in inverse proportion to the square of speed.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Induced drag falls as speed increases, so it rises as speed is reduced.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Induced drag depends on the lift coefficient, which rises as speed falls.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Induced drag is greatest at high angles of attack near the stall.

question_text: If airspeed is doubled, by what factor does parasite drag change, other factors remaining the same?

choices.text: It halves

subject: Principles of Flight
question_text: A pilot rolls into a left turn using ailerons alone. In which direction does adverse yaw tend to move the nose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To the right, away from the turn

choices.label: B
choices.text: To the left, into the turn

choices.label: C
choices.text: Downwards, with no yaw

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no yaw with ailerons alone

explanation: The down-going aileron on the rising (right) wing increases its lift and induced drag. The extra drag pulls the right wing back, yawing the nose right, away from the intended turn.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Adverse yaw opposes the turn; that is why rudder is co-ordinated with aileron.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Adverse yaw is a yawing, not a pitching, effect.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Unequal induced drag between the two wings does produce yaw.

question_text: The tab on an elevator trim system is deflected downwards. What is the effect on the elevator and the aeroplane's pitch?

subject: Principles of Flight
learning_objective: Relate CG position to longitudinal stability
question_text: What happens to longitudinal stability when the centre of gravity moves towards its aft limit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases, and stick forces become heavier

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is unaffected; only the stall speed changes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It decreases, and the aeroplane becomes more sensitive in pitch

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases, and stall recovery becomes easier

explanation: Longitudinal static stability depends on the distance between the CG and the neutral point. Moving the CG aft reduces that margin, lightening stick forces and reducing stability.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A forward CG increases stability and stick forces.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: CG position directly affects longitudinal stability.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: An aft CG reduces stability and can make stall or spin recovery harder.

question_text: Air flows through a venturi. In the narrowest section, compared with the entrance:

choices.label: A

choices.text: Speed is lower and static pressure is higher

question_text: Seen from the cockpit, an aeroplane's propeller rotates clockwise. Which way does the torque reaction tend to roll the aeroplane?

choices.text: To the right

choices.text: To the left

choices.text: Nose up

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Newton's third law applies; the airframe tends to rotate opposite to the propeller.

subject: Principles of Flight
question_text: Why is washout (a reduction in angle of incidence towards the wing tip) built into many wings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: So that the wing tip stalls before the root

choices.label: B
choices.text: To increase the maximum speed

choices.label: C
choices.text: So that the wing root stalls before the tip and aileron control is kept for longer

choices.label: D
choices.text: To increase lateral stability in cruise

explanation: Because the tip has a lower angle of incidence, the root reaches the critical angle of attack first. Air over the outboard ailerons stays attached longer, which helps roll control and gives a gentler stall.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Tip-first stalls are undesirable because they cause roll-off and loss of aileron control.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Washout is a stall-behaviour feature, not a speed feature.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Dihedral, not washout, is the main source of lateral stability.

question_text: How does the design manoeuvring speed (VA) change when the aeroplane's mass is reduced?

choices.text: It stays the same
